prompt:
Write a narrative account of about 500 words of the Boston molasses flood of 1919. The reader is a general reader.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists.

Write it in this voice: Calm, even register. Mostly medium-length, complete sentences, with length set by content rather than rhythm. No pattern of a short hook paid off by a longer sentence. Plain words over writerly ones, and lines allowed to sit flat. Numbers, names and concrete facts carry the point instead of abstractions. Em dashes, parentheticals, adverbs, doublets and parallelism kept rare. Descriptive writing states what a thing is and does, and any view is labelled as a view. British spelling.

text:
On 15 January 1919, a Tuesday, the temperature in Boston rose to about 4 degrees Celsius after several days of bitter cold. At the Purity Distilling Company's storage tank on Commercial Street, in the North End, that mild afternoon was the last ordinary one. The tank stood about 15 metres high and 27 metres across and held roughly 2.3 million gallons of molasses, which was a little over 8,700 cubic metres. The molasses had arrived by ship from the Caribbean and was destined to be fermented into industrial alcohol, a good deal of it for munitions during the war. The tank had been built in 1915 in a hurry. It was filled to the brim only a few times, and it leaked so badly that neighbours collected the syrup that ran down its sides. The company's response was to paint the tank brown, so that the stains showed less.

At about 12.30 in the afternoon, people nearby heard a rumbling sound and a series of sharp noises that several of them compared to machine-gun fire. These were the rivets shearing as the tank wall gave way. A wave of molasses, which witnesses and later estimates put at about 7.5 metres at its front, moved out across the neighbourhood at an estimated 55 kilometres an hour. It broke the supports of the elevated railway on Atlantic Avenue and pushed a firehouse off its foundations. It crushed or carried off houses, wagons and a number of horses. Parts of the tank itself were thrown against nearby buildings.

Twenty-one people died, and about 150 were injured. The dead included children and several city workers who were eating lunch near the firehouse. The molasses was cold and thick, and anyone caught in it found it hard to move. Rescuers waded in and found that it clung to their legs and clothes. Some victims were trapped for hours, and the work of recovering bodies went on for days. Police, firemen, soldiers and sailors from a nearby ship took part, and the Red Cross set up a base to treat the injured.

The clean-up took weeks. Fire crews pumped seawater and salt water over the streets, and sand and sawdust were spread to absorb what remained. The harbour ran brown until the summer. Residents said for years afterwards that the area smelled of molasses on warm days.

A long legal case followed. Purity Distilling argued that anarchists had blown up the tank, a claim that fitted the fears of the postwar years. The court appointed an auditor, Hugh Ogden, who heard evidence for about three years. He found that the tank had been poorly designed and inspected, and that the company had not tested it properly. The company was held liable, and it paid out roughly 600,000 dollars in settlements, which came to about 7,000 dollars for each of the families of the dead.

The disaster is often cited as a reason for later building regulations. Massachusetts began to require that architects and engineers approve large structures, and that their plans be filed with the state. Many engineers have since pointed to the case as an early lesson in structural safety.
